title: Founder case: Spanx and a problem the founder had

sources.claim: Sara Blakely cut the feet off control-top pantyhose to wear under white pants, started Spanx in 2000 with $5,000 of her savings, was turned down by hosiery manufacturers before one agreed, and got the product into Neiman Marcus.

sections.skill: Apply a documented decision: your own problem, then evidence others share it

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what problem did Blakely start with?

choices.text: She wanted to open a factory for making fabric.
She wanted cheaper shoes for running on trails.
She wanted a new kind of store for selling dresses.
She wanted a smooth look under white pants.

questions.correct_answer: She wanted a smooth look under white pants.
questions.intro: Documented history: Sara Blakely cut the feet off control-top pantyhose to wear under white pants. She started Spanx in 2000 with $5,000 of her own savings. Several hosiery manufacturers turned her down before one agreed to make the product, and she got it into the Neiman Marcus department store. Lesson drawn by this course (an interpretation, not her words): a problem you have yourself can be a starting point, but you still need evidence that many others share it and will buy. One success story does not guarantee the same result.

sections.skill: One person's problem versus a market

questions.prompt: Your own frustration with a product is best described as what?

choices.text: A clue worth checking
A guarantee of sales
Proof of a large market
A finished business plan

questions.intro: Your own problem is a clue, not proof. If you are frustrated by something, ask: do many other people have this same frustration, and do they spend money on it? One person is a sample of one. A market is many people with the same need who will pay. You find out by asking others about their experience and by testing whether they will buy, not by assuming they feel what you feel.
questions.feedback: Your own problem is a starting clue.
